## A kill is defined by four rules, and the script enforces all four

1. the owning test PASSED unmutated in the same run
2. the patch actually CHANGED the file
3. the run served the MUTATED code (bundle hash moved, and the red run is not a build or server failure)
4. a patch that does not compile is DOES NOT BUILD and is never a kill

## Each mutation in full

### `M1-decrypt-always-returns-plaintext`

**What it changes.** `open()` ignores the key it is handed and returns whatever `close()` last locked, so any private key appears to open the lock.

**Why this one.** This is the mutation a round-trip test cannot see, which is why the brief names it. Encrypt-then-decrypt still returns the message; Step 3's OPENED verdict is unchanged; the claims test that checks the recovered note still passes. What breaks is the REFUSAL, which is the only thing a lock actually promises. The unit suite's cross-pair rejection catches it too, and that redundancy is deliberate - the browser verdict and the algorithmic test are two independent witnesses to the same property.

**What the page then shows.** OPENED WITH THE WRONG KEY, in the alarm tone - the one state on this page that earns an alarm, because something that had to fail did not.

**Patch sites.** `src/crypto/lock.ts`, `src/crypto/lock.ts`, `src/crypto/lock.ts` (3 sites, each anchored on text that occurs exactly once).

**Owning test.** `Step 3 wrong key is refused CALMLY, and the page names the cause` — asserts the `wrong-key` verdict marker.

**Outcome: KILLED.** Baseline passed: true. Bundle 5ecf81a27aae278b → e2e3df926d6db82c.

### `M2-verify-always-accepts`

**What it changes.** `check()` runs the real verification and then discards its answer, returning true.

**Why this one.** Every signing round-trip stays green - a real signature still verifies - and so does Step 4's VERIFIED verdict. What breaks is the tamper path: one character changed and the check accepts it anyway. The page is built to paint that as an alarm rather than a pass, so the mutation is visible in the verdict tone as well as in the headline.

**What the page then shows.** VERIFIED THE TAMPERED TEXT, in the alarm tone.

**Patch sites.** `src/crypto/sign.ts` (1 site, each anchored on text that occurs exactly once).

### `M3-wrong-key-path-reuses-right-key`

**What it changes.** Step 3's wrong-key button generates a second pair, prints its genuinely different fingerprint, and then opens the lock with the READER'S OWN private half.

**Why this one.** The subtlest of the three and the one a careless implementation really produces, because nothing about it looks wrong: a fresh pair IS generated, so the two fingerprints on screen genuinely differ and the panel reads exactly as intended. Only the key handed to `open` is the wrong one. Every unit test stays green - this is a UI wiring defect, not a cryptographic one - so the browser verdict is the only witness.

**What the page then shows.** OPENED WITH THE WRONG KEY, in the alarm tone, beside two fingerprints that really are different.

**Patch sites.** `src/ui/step3.ts`, `src/ui/step3.ts` (2 sites, each anchored on text that occurs exactly once).

### `M4-negative-claim-text-deleted`

**What it changes.** The negative-claim sentence is emptied, so the fixture renders with no statement of the limitation it exists to demonstrate.

**Why this one.** §4.1d requires exactly this check: delete the negative-claim text and the assertion that it is on screen must fail. Note what does NOT break - the fixture still reaches its state, every verdict is still green, and the verdict still reads OPENED - AND UNATTRIBUTED - so nothing but the claim assertion can catch it. A negative-claim test that survives its own text being deleted is decorative.

**What the page then shows.** The fixture state exactly as it ships, minus the one sentence that makes it a result rather than a curiosity.

**Patch sites.** `src/ui/step3.ts` (1 site, each anchored on text that occurs exactly once).

**Owning test.** `every check passes, and the message is unattributed anyway` — asserts the `unattributed` verdict marker.

**Outcome: KILLED.** Baseline passed: true. Bundle 5ecf81a27aae278b → eb232fa3ea4e4393.

### `M5-fixture-check-broken`

**What it changes.** The stranger's block is opened with a freshly generated private half instead of the reader's, so the fixture's own decryption fails.

**Why this one.** The other half of what §4.1d requires: break a check inside the fixture and the assertion that everything is green must fail. The page then renders THE FIXTURE DID NOT HOLD, which is the honest outcome - a fixture whose own checks fail is demonstrating the mechanism working rather than its limit, and must never be allowed to read as a demonstration of the limitation.

**What the page then shows.** THE FIXTURE DID NOT HOLD, in the alarm tone, with no recovered text and no negative claim.

**Patch sites.** `src/ui/step3.ts` (1 site, each anchored on text that occurs exactly once).

**Owning test.** `every check passes, and the message is unattributed anyway` — asserts the `unattributed` verdict marker.

**Outcome: KILLED.** Baseline passed: true. Bundle 5ecf81a27aae278b → afb2454dd3f1e8dd.
